newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Pop star Geldof returns to Africa for Child Day.
newsitem.headline: Pop star Geldof returns to Africa for Child Day.

text.p: Pop celebrity Bob Geldof, who raised $130 million for Ethiopia famine victims in 1984, returned to the Horn of Africa on Monday for the Day of the African Child.
Geldof boarded a traditional dhow boat to watch children in this Somali coastal town float bottles into the sea with messages setting out their hopes.
"It was interesting what the kids actually said in their bottles -- they were identical to any person on the planet," Geldof told reporters.

"They want their mums and dads to be well. They want to be healthy. They want a good education and they have professional ambitions," said the Irish singer, who was given an honorary knighthood by Britain's Queen Elizabeth.
"It's the loftiness of the ambitions which is so surprising. It's fantastic," Geldof said in Bossaso, a town of 100,000 now being rebuilt after civil war.

The U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF) organised a conference on the media's role in emergencies to celebrate the Day of the African Child, started by the Organisation of African Unity in 1991 to commemorate the first child victim of South Africa's 1976 Soweto riots.
The conference heard tributes to legendary cameraman Mohamed Amin whose TV footage drew attention to the Ethiopia famine in 1984.
Amin, who worked for Reuters Television, died last November when a hijacked Ethiopian Airlines plane crashed off the Comoros islands.

"The African Child was a driving force for my father's work. He used his considerable energy and resources to try to bring the plight of the children of Africa to the attention of the world," Amin's son Salim Amin said.
"You would readily know that 'Mo' Amin was behind the camera because he had an unerring subjective eye of outrage and a 3-D, almost mystical, chemistry of light and passion mixed," Geldof said.
Geldof's Band Aid Trust combining Band Aid and Live Aid raised $130 million for victims of the 1984 Ethiopia famine and spawned a genre of pop events to raise money for disasters.
Mohamed Abshir Waldo, Secretary General of the Somali Salvation Democratic Front that controls Bossaso, blamed declining media interest in Somalia for a lack of aid funds.

"What the Somalis need are meaningful programmes and strategic engagement in our long-term rehabilitation problems, not a revolving door sequence of short-term and apparently disconnected projects," said Waldo.
"When there is not much coverage of an African country donors forget or ignore it. Out of media sight, out of donor mind," he said.

The collapse of Somalia's education system has left nine out of ten children without access to basic education in the last five years, though Koranic schools have survived and are attended by most boys and girls, UNICEF said.
UNICEF said its 1997 funds for Somalia were down to $8.3 million compared to $15.2 million in 1996.
Somalia has been without effective government since 1991 when late president Siad Barre was overthrown. Famine fuelled by the civil war that followed killed an estimated 300,000 in 1992.
